doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Writing the Top Ten for Renee Fleming with Tom Malone
summary: Shaffer describes preparing opera-parody numbers with Renee Fleming, Tom Malone arranging, and his shortcomings with the written page.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you had a guest like Renee Fleming, oh yow, speaking of learning on the job, was that a challenge? I think your buddy Tom “Bones” Malone related a story about how that occurred.

Certainly it was challenging for me. Again when you’re dealing with the written page, it’s not my forte. Nonetheless I was having to run this thing, and luckily Tom was not booked and was able to write the key arrangements for me that we needed. But first of all it’s Renee Fleming sings the Top Ten in some way. Now I can’t quite remember whether it was special lyrics, our writer, who shall remain nameless right now although he did a marvelous job, but I said you know in a case like Renee Fleming let’s see what songs she feels comfortable with changing the words to, and then let’s write in our jokes after that. And this writer didn’t think that was the way to go. He said, “No I have some choices here.” Okay. So he actually wrote the ones that he wanted. And I then had to learn what he’s done and the numbers ten through one different snatches of operas, well known operas, some more well known to this writer than to me I’ll tell you that, but nonetheless it’s only eight bars of each thing, and each one is hopefully a joke. That’s the way the Top Ten is going to be structured. And Renee said can someone send me a tape of the phrasing so I know how to deliver these things if you’re changing the lyrics. And so I made her that tape, happy to sing the stuff myself you know, as I would — oh I’m getting a call — you know I have — I just made three cents from this ringtone of “It’s Raining Men.”
I was going to ask you about the residuals.
Three cents at a time, believe me it mounts up. It’s great. What were we talking about? I’ve gotten thrown off.
Talking about Renee Fleming and you —

Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, she mentioned it. She says, “I’ve got a tape of you singing those ten songs in full voice whatever that means. To me it was just really a day’s work but then Tom was able to take my tape and arrange it and he did a beautiful job and we brought in special — you know he asked for a bassoon I think and an oboe. New York is the kind of © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

place where you just make one call and they’re there at 10 AM. Renee Fleming came into my dressing room, we had our little woodwind ensemble Chez — I don’t know if Chez was with us on that day or not anymore, but parts for everybody thanks to Tom, who stayed up all night writing these things, and then Renee making sure that she could time them right. Because it’s got to be camera goes back to Dave, he says, “Number seven” bang back to Renee who is now singing it. So really when he’s saying “Number seven” I’m going to be counting off the next thing and she said right, go ahead. You know. She was right on top of it and I don’t know who else could have done it really besides her. So it was quite gratifying by the end of it but certainly yes, challenging given my shortcomings when it comes to the written page especially. Because she could say in bar seven, “Paul, what is this in bar seven?” You know?
And I was just, “Tom —” I’ve learned how to, you know, just go to someone else.
